name: user_proxy
content:
PREVIOUS EXPLORATION:

Hypothesis: Patients receiving postoperative pharmaceutical therapy exhibit distinct gene co-expression network modules enriched for chemotherapy metabolism pathways compared to untreated patients.

Experiment objective: Use a full WGCNA‐style pipeline to identify gene co‐expression modules in breast cancer RNA-Seq data and test their associations with postoperative pharmaceutical therapy while adjusting for age and pathologic stage, then perform pathway enrichment on significant modules focusing on drug metabolism.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Load the two data files:
   • cleaned_gene_expression.csv (log2(FPKM+0.001) for ~60k genes × 1068 samples)
   • cleaned_clinical_data.csv (clinical metadata for 1097 patients)
   Align sample IDs by truncating expression column names to the first 12 characters to match bcr_patient_barcode.

2. Define analysis cohort:
   • Retain only samples where pharmaceutical_therapy is “YES” or “NO”.
   • Create a binary treatment vector (1=YES, 0=NO).
   • Extract age_at_diagnosis (numeric) and pathologic_stage (e.g., Stage I, IIA, IIB, IIIA, IIIB, IV); encode stage as dummy variables or ordinal numeric values.

3. Gene filtering:
   • Compute variance of each gene across retained samples.
   • Select the top 5,000 most variable genes to reduce noise and computation.

4. Soft‐threshold power selection:
   • For a range of candidate powers (e.g., 1–20), compute the adjacency matrix for each power using adjacency_ij = |cor(cori,j)|^power.
   • For each power, calculate the scale‐free topology fit index and mean connectivity.
   • Choose the smallest power that achieves a scale‐free fit index ≥0.85 (or the inflection point in the fit vs power curve) while maintaining adequate mean connectivity.

5. Adjacency and TOM calculation:
   • Using the chosen power, compute the adjacency matrix.
   • Convert adjacency to the topological overlap matrix (TOM) and derive TOM‐based dissimilarity (1 – TOM).

6. Module detection:
   • Perform hierarchical clustering on genes using TOM dissimilarity.
   • Apply dynamic tree cut (minModuleSize=30) to define initial modules and merge modules with eigengene correlation >0.75 (mergeCutHeight=0.25).

7. Module eigengenes:
   • For each module, calculate the module eigengene (first principal component of the scaled expression matrix of its genes).
   • Assemble an eigengene matrix (samples × modules).

8. Association testing:
   • For each module eigengene, fit a linear model: eigengene ~ treatment + age_at_diagnosis + (stage dummy variables).
   • Extract the coefficient, t‐statistic, and p‐value for the treatment term.
   • Adjust module p‐values for multiple testing using the Benjamini‐Hochberg procedure (FDR).

9. Identify significant modules:
   • Select modules with treatment‐term FDR < 0.05.

10. Pathway enrichment:
   • For each significant module, take its gene list and perform pathway enrichment (e.g., via Enrichr or similar) against the KEGG_2019_Human gene sets.
   • Filter enrichment results for drug metabolism and related pathways (e.g., “Drug metabolism – cytochrome P450”, “ABC transporters”, “Glutathione metabolism”).

11. Visualization and reporting:
   • Plot scale‐free topology fit vs power curve and mean connectivity vs power curve.
   • Plot the gene dendrogram colored by final module assignments.
   • Produce a module‐trait heatmap showing the correlation between module eigengenes and treatment, age, and stage (with p‐values).
   • For each significant module, present the KEGG drug metabolism enrichment bar plot.


Deliverables:
1. A plot of scale‐free topology fit index and mean connectivity across candidate powers, with chosen power annotated.
2. A table of gene‐to‐module assignments for the 5,000 filtered genes.
3. A matrix of module eigengenes (samples × modules) and their corresponding clinical covariates.
4. A results table for each module: module ID, number of genes, treatment effect estimate, t‐statistic, p‐value, FDR.
5. A module‐trait heatmap showing correlations and p‐values for treatment, age, and stage.
6. For each module with FDR < 0.05, a table of KEGG enrichment results filtered for drug metabolism pathways (Term, overlap, adjusted p‐value), plus corresponding bar plots.
7. Gene dendrogram with dynamic tree cut modules and merged module color annotations.

Analysis:
The pipeline completed successfully. 5,000 top variable genes were clustered into 9 modules, module eigengenes were computed, and linear models (adjusting for age and stage) tested treatment effects. Two modules had nominal p < 0.05 but none passed FDR < 0.05, so no pathway enrichment was performed. All deliverables—inclusive of power selection plot, module definitions, eigengene–trait tests, and visualizations—were generated.

Review:
Hypothesis: Patients receiving postoperative pharmaceutical therapy may harbor distinct gene co-expression modules enriched for drug metabolism pathways.

The revised pipeline now implements a full WGCNA-inspired workflow: 
– Filtered to 5,000 most variable genes.
– Selected soft-threshold power based on scale-free fit and mean connectivity.
– Computed adjacency and TOM, performed hierarchical clustering, and applied dynamic tree cut (via cutreeHybrid) with subsequent module merging (eigengene correlation >0.75). Final network yielded 9 modules (sizes 39–1883 genes).
– Calculated module eigengenes and tested their association with treatment status in linear models adjusting for age and pathologic stage. Two modules showed nominal significance (p<0.05), but none remained significant after FDR correction (smallest FDR=0.167).
– No modules met FDR < 0.05, so no drug metabolism pathway enrichment was detected.

All specified deliverables were produced: scale-free topology plots; gene-to-module assignments; module eigengene–trait association table including FDR; module–trait heatmap; and gene dendrogram with module colors. The negative result indicates no pharmaceutical therapy–associated modules at FDR < 0.05.

name: user_proxy
content:
PREVIOUS EXPLORATION:

Hypothesis: Patients with a higher burden of high-impact somatic mutations (IMPACT = HIGH) exhibit shorter disease-free survival (time to new tumor event) after initial treatment.

Experiment objective: Quantify per-patient count of high-impact mutations and test its association with disease-free survival, adjusting for age and stage.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Load cleaned_mutations.csv and cleaned_clinical_data.csv; merge on bcr_patient_barcode.
2. Filter mutations to those with IMPACT == 'HIGH'; count high-impact mutations per patient to define a mutation burden variable.
3. From clinical data, extract new_tumor_event (YES/NO), days_to_new_tumor, age_at_diagnosis, and pathologic_stage (encode as dummy variables or ordinal numeric).
4. Construct a survival object where time = days_to_new_tumor, event = (new_tumor_event == 'YES').
5. Fit a Cox proportional hazards model: Surv(time, event) ~ highImpactBurden + age_at_diagnosis + pathologic_stage.
6. Test the hazard ratio and p-value for the highImpactBurden term; check proportional hazards assumptions.
7. Optionally, dichotomize highImpactBurden at median and plot Kaplan–Meier curves for high vs low groups with log-rank test.

Deliverables:
• Table of high-impact mutation counts per patient.
• Cox model summary (hazard ratios, 95% CIs, p-values).
• Proportional hazards assumption diagnostics.
• Kaplan–Meier plot comparing high vs low high-impact burden groups and log-rank test p-value.

Analysis:
The code successfully loaded and merged mutation and clinical data, computed per‐patient high‐impact mutation counts (n=1,097), and constructed a disease‐free survival dataset (n=923 patients, 7 events). A Cox model adjusting for age and pathologic stage yielded a non‐significant effect of highImpactBurden (HR≈0.98, p=0.63). Convergence warnings reflect very low event counts and complete separation in some stage strata; the proportional hazards test flagged stage_Stage IIIA (p≈0.04) for non‐proportionality. Dichotomized Kaplan–Meier curves (High vs Low burden) produced a log‐rank p=0.1334, indicating no significant difference in disease‐free survival. Overall, there is no evidence that higher high‐impact mutation burden shortens disease‐free survival.

Review:
Hypothesis: Patients with more high-impact mutations have shorter disease-free survival. The implementation followed the experimental plan: merged clinical and mutation data, counted high-impact mutations per patient, constructed survival outcomes, fitted a Cox model adjusting for age and stage, checked proportional hazards, and plotted KM curves with log-rank test. Results: HighImpactBurden coefficient was non-significant (HR≈0.98, p=0.63); only 7 events in 923 patients limiting power; assumption test flagged one stage variable for non-proportionality. The log-rank test for high vs low burden was non-significant (p=0.133). No evidence supports the hypothesis under current data constraints.

Hypothesis: Global tumor heterogeneity captured by the second principal component of gene expression predicts overall survival independent of stage and age.

Experiment objective: To evaluate whether PC2 of expression data is an independent predictor of overall survival.

Steps for the programmer:
1. Load cleaned_gene_expression.csv and cleaned_clinical_data.csv; align barcodes.
2. Filter to patients with complete vital_status, days_to_death, days_to_last_followup, age_at_diagnosis, and pathologic_stage.
3. Select the top 5,000 most variable genes, standardize, and perform PCA.
4. Extract PC2 scores per patient.
5. Construct a survival object: time = days_to_death if dead else days_to_last_followup, event = (vital_status=='Dead').
6. Create a clinical dataframe with PC2, age_at_diagnosis, pathologic_stage encoded as dummies.
7. Fit a multivariate Cox proportional hazards model: Surv(time,event) ~ PC2 + age_at_diagnosis + pathologic_stage.
8. Check proportional hazards assumptions.
9. Plot adjusted survival curves for high vs low PC2 (dichotomized at median).
10. Report hazard ratio and p-value for PC2.

Deliverables:
• Patient-level PC2 scores with survival data.
• Cox model summary (HR, 95% CI, p-values).
• Diagnostics for proportional hazards.
• Kaplan–Meier plot comparing high vs low PC2 groups with log-rank p-value.

# Compute follow-up time
clinical['time'] = clinical.apply(
    lambda r: r['days_to_death'] if r['vital_status']=='Dead' else r['days_to_last_followup'], axis=1)
# Drop incomplete
clinical = clinical.dropna(subset=['time', 'age_at_diagnosis', 'pathologic_stage', 'vital_status'])

# 3. Align samples
common = clinical['bcr_patient_barcode'].unique()
expr = expr.loc[:, expr.columns.intersection(common)]
clinical = clinical.set_index('bcr_patient_barcode').loc[expr.columns]
print(f"Number of patients for analysis: {len(clinical)}")

# 4. Filter top 5000 most variable genes
gene_var = expr.var(axis=1)
top_genes = gene_var.nlargest(5000).index
expr_top = expr.loc[top_genes]

# 5. PCA on standardized expression (samples x genes)
X = expr_top.T.values  # shape: (n_samples, 5000)
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X)
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
pcs = pca.fit_transform(X_scaled)
# PC2 is index 1
pc2 = pcs[:, 1]

# 6. Build Cox model dataframe
df_cox = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        'PC2': pc2,
        'age_at_diagnosis': clinical['age_at_diagnosis'].astype(float),
        'time': clinical['time'].astype(float),
        'event': (clinical['vital_status']=='Dead').astype(int),
        'pathologic_stage': clinical['pathologic_stage']
    },
    index=clinical.index
)
# One-hot encode stage
stage_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df_cox['pathologic_stage'], prefix='stage', drop_first=True)
df_cox2 = pd.concat([df_cox.drop('pathologic_stage', axis=1), stage_dummies], axis=1)

# 7. Fit Cox proportional hazards model
cph = CoxPHFitter()
cph.fit(df_cox2, duration_col='time', event_col='event')
print("\nCox model summary:")
print(cph.summary)

# 8. Proportional hazards diagnostics
print("\nChecking proportional hazards assumptions:")
cph.check_assumptions(df_cox2, show_plots=False)

# 9. Kaplan-Meier by PC2 median split
median_pc2 = df_cox2['PC2'].median()
high = df_cox2[df_cox2['PC2'] > median_pc2]
low  = df_cox2[df_cox2['PC2'] <= median_pc2]
kmf_high = KaplanMeierFitter()
kmf_low  = KaplanMeierFitter()
plt.figure()
kmf_high.fit(high['time'], event_observed=high['event'], label='PC2 High')
ax = kmf_high.plot(ci_show=False)
kmf_low.fit(low['time'], event_observed=low['event'], label='PC2 Low')
kmf_low.plot(ax=ax, ci_show=False)
plt.title('Survival by PC2 Group')
plt.xlabel('Time (days)')
plt.ylabel('Survival Probability')

# Log-rank test
lr = logrank_test(high['time'], low['time'], event_observed_A=high['event'], event_observed_B=low['event'])
print(f"\nLog-rank test p-value: {lr.p_value:.4f}")
plt.show()"}
